1.pericope_label: And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word. And the word of the Lord came unto him, saying, Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan. And it shall be, that thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there. So he went and did according unto the word of the Lord: for he went and dwelt by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan. And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook. And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the Greek reading of the prophet's origin, of Tishbe in Gilead, the last words added to distinguish it from the Naphtali Tishbe, whose mention he thinks textually doubtful, and notes that the word rendered inhabitants properly means sojourners and shares a derivation with Tishbite, while the alternative, the stranger of the strangers of Gilead, is doubtful Hebrew. He places Cherith east of Jordan, from the prophet's own country. On the ravens he is emphatic: the plain rendering is that of almost all the ancient versions and of Josephus, and the singularly prosaic substitutes got by altering the vowel points, Arabs or merchants or the inhabitants of a city Orbi or the rock Oreb, arise from a desire to be rid of a strange miracle and pay for it with a gross improbability, since regular sustenance by human hands could not have gone on under the king's jealous vigilance. Delitzsch explains the hiding not as flight but as policy, since the prophet had said the rain would come at his word and would have been urged to order it to come, and holds that the Hebrew leaves it undetermined whether Cherith lay east or west of Jordan.

Gill says it is not easy to say why Elijah is called the Tishbite, prefers Kimchi's account that he was first of a city called Toshab and afterwards dwelt in Gilead, and identifies that city with the Thisbe in Naphtali. He takes the concealment simply as flight from danger, Ahab and Jezebel having been provoked by the prophet's reproofs, and on the provisions thinks the source need not be inquired into, though he passes on the Jewish guesses that they came from Ahab's table, or Jehoshaphat's, or from the tables of the seven thousand who had not bowed the knee.

Clarke entertains at length the opinion that Elijah had no earthly parentage but was an angel united for a time to a human body, even asking whether the name, which signifies he is my God, countenances a manifestation in the flesh of the Supreme Being, before conceding that the apostle's description of him as a man of like passions is irreconcilable with it. He takes the hiding as ordinary prudence, since on the first drought Ahab would have sought the prophet's life, reports both opinions about the site of Cherith, notes a Greek manuscript and some fathers reading bread in the morning and flesh in the evening against all other versions, and calls this the first account of flesh at breakfast and supper.

Henry observes that where a prophet usually enters with parentage and tribe, Elijah drops out of the clouds as if, like Melchisedek, without father or descent, which made some Jews fancy him an angel; but the apostle assures us he was a man of like passions, which Henry thinks may intimate a temper hotter than most, fitting him for the daring sinners of his age, since rough spirits are called to rough services and the reformation needed such a man as Luther to break the ice. He denies that the concealment was chiefly for the prophet's safety, since it does not appear Ahab immediately sought him, and makes it a judgment on a people who would otherwise have had his instruction and intercession. On the ravens he multiplies reasons why these birds in particular: they are birds of prey likelier to take his meat than bring it, unclean by the law, carrion-feeders bringing wholesome food, neglectful of their own young, and themselves fed by special providence.

positions.position: Tishbe in Gilead, the Naphtali Tishbe being a different and textually doubtful place
Originally of a city called Toshab, identified with the Thisbe in Naphtali, and afterwards of Gilead

debates.question: Why was Elijah told to hide?

For safety, since Ahab would have sought his life at the first drought

8.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto him, saying, Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee. So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, the widow woman was there gathering of sticks: and he called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink. And as she was going to fetch it, he called to her, and said, Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thine hand. And she said, As the Lord thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die. And Elijah said unto her, Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son. For thus saith the Lord God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the Lord sendeth rain upon the earth. And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days. And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by Elijah.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the clause about Zidon as emphatic, marking a providence that found welcome in the native place of the prophet's deadliest foe, and places Zarephath on the great coast-road. He offers two accounts of whether the famine had reached so far, that it may have, one authority making it last a year in that country, or that the distress may have been only the reflex of the famine in Israel, on which the country depended for supplies. On the widow's oath he holds that the words thy God imply she did not yet acknowledge the God of Israel as her own, and he calls the sustaining miracle doubly remarkable: that God's higher laws of miracle, like the ordinary laws of providence, take in the supply of homely and trivial needs, the opposite of what expectation would suggest; and that it is a miracle of multiplication, virtual creation though not out of nothing, doing rapidly and directly what ordinary law does slowly and indirectly.

Gill takes the sending as a trial of Elijah's faith, to be lodged among Zidonians where Jezebel had an interest, and records that Kimchi denied the place was Gentile at all, reading the phrase as near to Zidon rather than belonging to it. Against Ellicott he takes the widow's oath by the living God to show her already a good woman, swearing by him only and taking Elijah for a prophet, and he compares the increase of the meal to the loaves multiplying while the disciples ate.

Clarke locates Zarephath between Tyre and Sidon but nearer the latter, gives its present name as Sarphan, and reports a traveller who found only a few houses on the mountain tops but supposed the old city stood in the plain below among ruins. He insists the barrel is an earthen jar and not a wooden vessel, since in the East corn and meal are kept so against the insects, says the word for cruse means a bottle, observes that the command to bake for the stranger first was putting the widow's faith to an extraordinary trial, and compares the miracle to the water at Cana found wine as it was drawn.

Henry makes most of the choice of a heathen city, since our Saviour notices it as an early indication of favour designed for the Gentiles, many widows being in Israel who would gladly have taken the prophet in; Israel having corrupted themselves worse than the nations, their casting off is justly the riches of the world, and Elijah driven out by his countrymen turns to the Gentiles as the apostles were afterwards ordered to do. He presses the choice of Sidon in particular, the Baal-worship now the crying sin of Israel having lately come thence with Jezebel, so that out of Sidon God calls the destroyer of that idolatry and hides his prophet in his enemy's own country. On the widow he asks what assurance she had that this stranger was a prophet, when a hungry vagrant might easily have imposed on her, and answers that great was her faith, exceeding all things considered that of the widow who cast in two mites; and he weighs the two miracles, holding the increase of her faith as great a work in the kingdom of grace as the increase of her oil in the kingdom of providence.

positions.position: Yes, and the point of the story, since the prophet is sent to a heathen city and becomes the first prophet of the Gentiles

17.pericope_label: And it came to pass after these things, that the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so sore, that there was no breath left in him. And she said unto Elijah, What have I to do with thee, O thou man of God? art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance, and to slay my son? And he said unto her, Give me thy son. And he took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into a loft, where he abode, and laid him upon his own bed. And he cried unto the Lord, and said, O Lord my God, hast thou also brought evil upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by slaying her son? And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the Lord, and said, O Lord my God, I pray thee, let this child’s soul come into him again. And the Lord heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived. And Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the chamber into the house, and delivered him unto his mother: and Elijah said, See, thy son liveth. And the woman said to Elijah, Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in thy mouth is truth.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears presumption in Elijah's complaint, calling it characteristic of the half-presumptuous impatience shown more fully two chapters later, and takes him to imply that his own hard lot as an unprotected fugitive must have brought trouble on the house that sheltered him. On the stretching he rejects the natural explanation by name: to suppose it merely the use of natural means of reviving is to explain the whole description away, the idea being of a healing virtue attaching in measure to the prophets as it belonged without measure to our Lord, though in their case made conditional on prayer. On the woman's last words he traces three stages of faith, from speaking of Jehovah from without as the Lord thy God, to recognising him as God, to accepting the word in the prophet's mouth as truth, which seems to express conversion. Delitzsch denies that the death was a punishment for particular sins at all, comparing the man born blind, while granting that she discerned a punishment in it and finding in that half-heathenish belief a mind susceptible to divine truth; he calls Elijah here the forerunner of him who raises all the dead.
Gill will only say that the mother spoke rashly, in her passion and agony, forgetting the benefits she had received through the prophet's presence.

Clarke takes the mother at her word, that she was conscious of some secret sin forgotten or passed over too carelessly and supposed her son's life taken to punish it, adding that it is mostly in adversity that we consider our moral state. On the stretching he holds the view Ellicott refuses, that Elijah did it to communicate warmth and dispose the body to receive the departed spirit. On what returned to the child he argues with himself, saying at the prayer that the soul means no more than the breath and at the fulfilment that the word generally means the immortal spirit, so that the expression is strong proof both that an immaterial spirit exists in man and that it can exist apart from the body, lying in the midst of him like a spring at the centre of a machine. He closes the chapter by reopening its beginning, arguing against the ravens on the ground that the bird is unclean and carrion-feeding and that the reading needs three miracles where God's way is the simplest means, and contending that the word may mean merchants, against Bochart's lexicography.

Henry reads the death as sin-related and generalises it, that when God removes our comforts he remembers our sins against us, perhaps the iniquities of our youth, so that our sins are the death of our children, and that he does so in order that we may remember and repent of them; he guesses the widow's former worship of Baal may be in view, and takes the affliction as a thorn in the flesh lest she be lifted up. Where Ellicott hears presumption in the prophet's complaint, Henry hears humble pleading, Elijah urging the greatness of the affliction to a widow and then his own concern, that if death follows him into the houses receiving him others will fear to entertain him. On the stretching he takes a third way, that the act was to affect Elijah himself with the case and to signify what God does by grace in raising dead souls, and on the soul's return he credits Grotius with thinking God designed the miracle to intimate the soul's separate existence and immortality.

debates.question: Was the child's death a punishment for the mother's sin?

positions.position: No; not for particular sins at all, but a medium for the manifestation of the works of God, as with the man born blind
Yes; she was conscious of some secret sin and supposed the life taken to punish it
Yes in the sense that God remembers our sins when he removes our comforts, so that we may repent of them
She spoke rashly in her passion, forgetting the benefits received

debates.question: What was Elijah doing when he stretched himself on the child?

positions.position: Not using natural means; a healing virtue attached to the prophets, though made conditional on prayer

Affecting himself with the case, and signifying what God does by grace in raising dead souls

debates.question: How should Elijah's complaint to God be heard?

positions.position: As half-presumptuous impatience, of a piece with his conduct two chapters later
As humble pleading, on the widow's behalf and on his own
